title: Warm Bluebook — Law Journal Argument Folio
description: A law-review-faithful slide that mirrors the typographic conventions of a bound journal page: Bluebook citation header at 10pt, bold-serif holding statement in oxblood, numbered reasoning paragraphs with superscript footnote markers, and a closing hairline rule anchoring two footnotes — indistinguishable in discipline from a Harvard Law Review column.
philosophy: This template exists because legal argument has its own typographic grammar, and that grammar is not negotiable. It treats the Bluebook citation string and the footnote separator as primary design elements, not decorative afterthoughts. It refuses drop shadows, color fields, icon sets, and anything that would look alien stapled into a law review volume. It is built for the scholar who must persuade through authority and structure, in a room where the audience reads footnotes.
goodFor: Moot court argument summaries requiring formal citation scaffolding
Law review symposia and article-preview presentations
Constitutional law or appellate advocacy classroom lectures
Case analysis slides where the holding must be visually dominant
avoidFor: Chart-heavy litigation analytics or evidentiary data dashboards
Client-facing business development or firm-branding decks
Presentations requiring image-forward or infographic layouts
Informal teaching contexts where dense serif columns lose the room
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like the opening recto of a bound law review volume — austere, credentialed, and unhurried. Compositional drama arrives through typographic scale alone: a compact citation header recedes so that the bold holding statement can claim the vertical center with the gravity of settled doctrine. The mood is deliberate restraint — no color field, no decorative mark, nothing that could not survive reproduction onto cream stock. Avoid any gesture toward corporate polish or modernist minimalism; the register is scholarly solemnity, not designed elegance.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with content occupying a centered 8-column text block and roughly 10% outer margins that echo journal trim size. A hairline rule separates the Bluebook citation string at the head from the dominant article-title field below; a second hairline rule closes the author/affiliation line before a spare footer. Hierarchy is resolved by scale contrast alone — citation string tight and tracked, holding title commanding the vertical center, author attribution reduced and set in italic. Volume identifier or page number anchors the bottom-right corner with no surrounding decoration.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a page torn from a bound law review volume — dense with authority, every element serving argument over ornament. Compositional rhythm is strictly vertical: citation string → holding declaration → numbered body → footnote zone, with hairline rules as the sole structural punctuation. The mood is austere and credentialed, evoking a moot court brief filed on cream stock. Avoid icons, tint bands, drop shadows, or anything that would look alien stapled between journal pages.

<!-- Running head / folio marker -->
<g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#7a7468" font-size="14" letter-spacing="2">
<text x="115" y="178">VOL. 137 · HARV. L. REV. · ARGUMENT FOLIO</text>
<text x="1805" y="178" text-anchor="end">PART II — § 4 · EXTRATERRITORIALITY</text>
</g>

<!-- Holding statement -->
<g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a">
<text x="115" y="270" font-size="46" font-weight="700">Held: The presumption against extraterritoriality</text>
<text x="115" y="324" font-size="46" font-weight="700">applies to claims brought under the Alien Tort</text>
<text x="115" y="378" font-size="46" font-weight="700">Statute, and nothing in the statute rebuts it.<tspan font-size="22" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">1</tspan></text>
</g>

<!-- Numbered reasoning paragraphs -->
<g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a" font-size="20">

<!-- Paragraph 1 -->
<text x="115" y="470"><tspan font-weight="700" fill="#7d2a2a">1.  </tspan><tspan font-weight="700">Textual Silence as Default Restraint.</tspan>  The ATS is a jurisdictional grant, not a substantive cause of action, and</text>
<text x="115" y="500">the canon disfavoring extraterritorial reach demands an affirmative congressional indication before federal courts may</text>
<text x="115" y="530">recognize private causes for conduct occurring on foreign soil. The First Congress legislated against a backdrop in which</text>
<text x="115" y="560">universal jurisdiction was reserved for piracy and a narrow class of offenses against ambassadors.<tspan font-size="14" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">2</tspan></text>

<!-- Paragraph 2 -->
<text x="115" y="618"><tspan font-weight="700" fill="#7d2a2a">2.  </tspan><tspan font-weight="700">Comity and the Avoidance Canon.</tspan>  Permitting suit for foreign-cubed conduct invites diplomatic friction the political</text>
<text x="115" y="648">branches are better positioned to manage; the avoidance canon counsels courts to read jurisdictional grants narrowly</text>
<text x="115" y="678">when broader readings would intrude upon foreign sovereignty or unsettle the executive's conduct of foreign affairs.<tspan font-size="14" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">3</tspan></text>

<!-- Paragraph 3 -->
<text x="115" y="736"><tspan font-weight="700" fill="#7d2a2a">3.  </tspan><tspan font-weight="700">Touch-and-Concern Threshold.</tspan>  Even where some domestic conduct is alleged, claims must "touch and concern"</text>
<text x="115" y="766">the territory of the United States with sufficient force to displace the presumption — mere corporate presence is</text>
<text x="115" y="796">insufficient, and the petitioners' allegations here do not clear that threshold under any plausible reading of the record.<tspan font-size="14" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">4</tspan></text>
</g>

<!-- Footnote zone -->
<g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a" font-size="15">
<text x="115" y="938"><tspan font-size="11" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">1</tspan> <tspan dx="4">Kiobel, 569 U.S. at 124. The Court declined to reach the corporate-liability question on which certiorari was originally granted, resolving the case on extraterritoriality grounds first raised at supplemental briefing.</tspan></text>
<text x="115" y="968"><tspan font-size="11" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">2</tspan> <tspan dx="4">See Sosa, 542 U.S. at 720; Anthony J. Bellia & Bradford R. Clark, </tspan><tspan font-style="italic">The Alien Tort Statute and the Law of Nations</tspan><tspan>, 78 U. Chi. L. Rev. 445, 461–67 (2011).</tspan></text>
<text x="115" y="998"><tspan font-size="11" baseline-shift="super" fill="#7d2a2a">3</tspan> <tspan dx="4">Morrison v. Nat'l Austl. Bank Ltd., 561 U.S. 247, 255 (2010); EEOC v. Arabian Am. Oil Co., 499 U.S. 244, 248 (1991).</tspan></text>

examples.layoutNotes: 12-col grid with content occupying cols 2–11 and a 6% outer margin on each side; the slide reads top-to-bottom as a single justified column. A Bluebook citation string sits at the very top, separated from the body by a hairline rule spanning the full content width. The holding statement occupies the upper body zone at roughly double the body measure, flush-left, followed by two or three numbered reasoning paragraphs carrying inline superscript footnote markers. A second hairline rule divides the lower body from a two-line footnote zone pinned to the bottom margin, with no page-number badge or decorative footer band.
